http://www.advertiser.ie/galway/article/.text: The ancestral village of Menlough, East Galway, will once again become the focal point for the global Mannion diaspora when it hosts the Thirteenth Annual International Mannion Clan Gathering from Friday, 14 August to Sunday, 16 August 2026. Coinciding with the opening of National Heritage Week, the three-day celebration promises a rich programme of history, culture, genealogy and traditional Irish heritage. Festivities begin on Friday evening at 7.00 pm in Thompson’s Pub, Menlough, with registration and a welcoming reception, offering visitors from Ireland and overseas an opportunity to meet fellow clansfolk. The official opening will be performed by Galway County Heritage Officer Marie Mannion, who will extend a welcome on behalf of Galway County Council. The opening evening also features an illustrated presentation on the history and heritage of the Mannion Clan by clan historian Dr Joe Mannion, tracing the story of the Ó Mainnín family through the centuries. The programme concludes with a performance of traditional Irish sean-nós dancing by champion dancer Meadhbh Ní Chualáin. Saturday’s events centre on a guided tour of the Mannion Clan Historical Trail, led by Dr Joe Mannion. Participants will gather at Frank Mannion’s Lounge Bar in Abbeyknockmoy before travelling to a number of sites closely associated with the clan’s remarkable past. Among the locations visited will be Killaclogher, Clooncurreen and the site of Menlough Castle, together with the ancient ceremonial mound at Ramore in Mullaghmore West. It was here, in May 1584, that a landmark agreement between the two principal branches of the Mannion Clan was drafted under Brehon Law by a Mac Egan lawyer. The tour will also include Ballymannion, a sub-townland central to the historic Ó Mainnín legal deed. Abbey visit Following refreshments in Menlough, the group will visit Kilconnell Abbey, where John, son of Malachy, the last recorded Chief of the Name of the Mannion Clan, was buried in 1648 alongside two of his kinsmen from the clan’s traditional stronghold of Mionlach Uí Mhainnín. The final stop will be at the battlefield of Finnure, near Loughrea, where the reigning Ó Mainnín king of Soghan was killed in AD 1135 during a fierce conflict between the O’Connors of Connacht and the O’Kellys of Hy Many. Local historian Paul O’Donnell will provide an historical account of the battle. Saturday evening returns to Thompson’s Lounge Bar, where Jim Hollarn, the clan’s genetic genealogist from San Diego, California, will present the latest developments in the Mannion Surname DNA Project. This will be followed by a family history and genealogy session with Noel Murphy and Peadar Ó Mainín of the Rosmuc Area Genealogy and DNA Group. The gathering concludes on Sunday with a full programme in Menlough, including a Clan Mass celebrated by Fr Colm Mannion OP, a piper-led international clan parade and an engaging presentation on medieval and early modern Irish clothing and weaponry by Proinsias Mag Fhionnghaile, chieftain and historian of the McGinley Clan. The weekend will finish with the annual Mannion Clan barbecue overlooking the site of the former Ó Mainnín chieftains’ castle, followed by a traditional Irish music session featuring Fr Colm Mannion, Alan Mannion and friends. Contributions from gathering participants will add a fitting finale to the celebrations. Visitors are expected from across Ireland as well as from the United States, Canada, England and Latvia, reflecting the worldwide reach of the Mannion family. While the gathering celebrates the history of the Mannion Clan, attendance is open to everyone with an interest in Irish heritage, local history or genealogy. Further information is available by emailing [email protected] . https://english.news.cn/20260924/17d9b11.text: Slovakia to halve 2nd-class train fares amid rising fuel prices Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-24 00:14:15 Photo taken with a mobile phone on Sept. 21, 2026 shows a train arriving at Main Railway Station in Bratisalva, Slovakia. Slovakia will cut second-class passenger train fares by 50 percent for one month starting from Oct. 1, Prime Minister Robert Fico announced Wednesday after a government meeting. (Xinhua/Liu Haodong) BRATISLAVA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Slovakia will cut second-class passenger train fares by 50 percent for one month starting from Oct. 1, Prime Minister Robert Fico announced Wednesday after a government meeting. The measure, approved on the proposal of the Slovakian Transport Ministry, will initially remain in effect for 30 days. Subsequently, it will be reviewed on a monthly basis, Fico said. "Slovakia is currently facing a sharp rise in fuel prices with a direct impact on the economy and households, whose costs for private car transport are increasing. One of the possible solutions is to shift from private car transport to passenger rail transport," the ministry said in its explanatory report. The measure is primarily intended for people who use trains regularly to commute to work or school, or for other daily needs. The 50 percent reduction will apply to all second-class, single-journey tickets, as well as weekly and monthly season tickets. The temporary fare reduction is expected to reduce railway operators' revenues by about 4.3 million euros (4.9 million U.S. dollars) over the 30-day period, while increasing their costs by around 1 million euros (1.14 million dollars). The government is also considering measures for regional bus transport. Slovakian Transport Minister Jozef Raz has been tasked with preparing by Sept. 30 a proposal under which the state will reimburse self-governing regions for one third of their spending on suburban bus services if they reduce fares by 30 percent. ■

https://www.dw.com/en/weapons-war-and-wa.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PmU2 Prefer DW on Google Chancellor Friedrich Merz has insisted on German support for Ukraine's war effort against Russia Image: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety. Long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a new survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation . In the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents said they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year. Growing numbers of Germans oppose international engagement Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September. The findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025. Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points." Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action. No longer a majority in favor of military aid to Ukraine The most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Currently, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether. As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). "Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer said. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine." The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls. Support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic). Overwhelming majority wants Germany to remain neutral between the US and China One finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US. This may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump . Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation said of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers." The picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach. "The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," said Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation. If Europe wants independence, why does it keep turning to the US? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Should Germany always stand by Israel? Now only a third agree One issue that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago. This may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?" The results were striking: 61% of respondents said no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%. This article was originally written in German.
